reading.body:
The American Bankers Association appears on 12 AI lobbying filings, and 32 lobbyists are named across them, with nine named on all 12.

The pattern is concentration at the top and a long tail below. Nine lobbyists appear on every filing, then the counts step down through 11, 8, 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2. That is the shape of a standing team carrying a single client's AI portfolio, with additional names brought in on particular filings. The filings are held under one client, the association itself, so this is trade-group advocacy rather than a company lobbying for its own products.

Banking is where AI governance and financial regulation meet. The same rules that would govern model risk, data use and automated decisions in lending or payments are written by the committees these filings reach. A trade group filing repeatedly on AI is a signal that its members expect the rules to be set soon and want a hand in the wording.

What the data does not say is what the association argued. A filing reports that a firm lobbied on an issue, not the position taken, so 12 filings establish attention and volume, not direction. The data also carries no dollar amounts, no agencies, no bill numbers and no dates beyond the filing set, and it says nothing about compute, data centers or electricity. Nothing here connects this lobbying to the grid constraint, and it should not be read as if it did.

summary: AMERICAN BANKERS ASSOCIATION filed 12 Lobbying Disclosure Act reports on AI held by this site. Its clients, the lobbyists named on those filings and the AI bills they name are below. LDA registrant id 1785.
